correctness.rationale: The semilattice lower-set-rank proof forces both theta and alpha grade preservation by two permutation sums. On each nilpotent G=P x Q, the Hall--Paige map beta on noncyclic P converts to beta^(k inverse mod exp P) because k is odd; CRT produces coprime exponents a and 1+ka for odd Q. A cyclic nontrivial P contributes its unique involution to the projected total product, contradicting U^k=1 for odd k. Trivial and boundary cases handled. Standalone finite verifier found 45 witnesses, 8 cyclic obstructions, 4 exhaustive Clifford instances and 765 CRT cases; these are supportive checks, not an all-orders proof.

originality.rationale: The 2026 primary text explicitly poses power-exponent existence for Clifford semigroups as Problem 15.8. Its group Hall--Paige theorem and inverse-semigroup theorem handle ordinary k=1, whereas the new statement classifies odd powers k>=3 with nilpotent local groups, proves preservation of each group fiber for all positive k, and supplies a product/CRT construction. The 1984 homonymous k-complete notion denotes cycle lengths, not powers. Targeted published-finding corpus and external literature searches found no theorem implying this combination; searches cannot prove universal novelty.
residual_risks: The literature search cannot exclude an older exact odd-power theorem under alternate orthomorphism or transversal terminology.
A broader nilpotent-to-nonnilpotent group-power classification might imply the group part even if not surfaced in available searches.
Hall--Paige is invoked as an established theorem rather than independently proved.

value.rationale: This solves the odd-exponent k>=3 existence question for the natural class of Clifford semigroups with nilpotent local groups singled out by 2026 Problem 15.8; it includes arbitrary finite semilattices, connecting homomorphisms and nonabelian nilpotent group fibers. It gives exact necessary and sufficient local Sylow-2 data, explicit constructive witnesses, and shows no cross-fiber permutation can evade an obstruction. This structural classification is not obtained from an arbitrary finite census or the k=1 Hall--Paige theorem alone.
